regime.assessment: The economy remains in Reflation with growth holding up and inflation re-accelerating, while the Fed is officially on hold. GDP growth is robust at 4.3% annualized (FRED:A191RL1Q225SBEA: 4.3) and Atlanta Fed GDPNow is tracking 2.9% (FRED:GDPNOW: 2.9), while payrolls rebounded to 165k (FRED:PAYEMS: 165) and initial claims dropped to 196k (FRED:IC4WSA: 196000). Simultaneously, headline CPI sits at 4.08% (FRED:CPIAUCSL: 4.08) and Core PCE is 3.26% (FRED:PCEPILFE: 3.26), well above the Fed's 2% objective. Statistical recession risk remains normal at p_12m=0.243 (CALC:recession_risk), supported by an un-inverted yield curve (10y-3m at +0.68) and a dormant Sahm rule at 0.0 (FRED:SAHMREALTIME: 0). However, pullback risk is elevated under the surface despite the model reading p_10pct_3m=0.149 (CALC:pullback_risk), as high-yield credit spreads have spiked sharply to 3.77% (z=+2.01, FRED:BAMLH0A0HYM2: 3.77), 1-month S&P realized volatility sits at the 96th percentile (CALC:risk_indicators), and VIX is elevated at 26.8 (FRED:VIXCLS: 26.8).

rates_10y.why: 10-year Treasury yield is at 4.85% (FRED:DGS10: 4.85), already near the top of its range (93.4th percentile). While the deficit is wide (-$2.11T, FRED:MTSDS133FMS) and CPI is 4.08% (FRED:CPIAUCSL: 4.08), the market has already aggressively priced Fed hawkishness into 2y yields (DGS2 at 4.61%, CALC:market_implied_fed_path) and breakevens remain anchored at 2.15% (FRED:T10YIE: 2.15). No strong directional catalyst to break beyond current market pricing.

oil.why: Physical oil markets are in steep backwardation (+7.4% front vs 6 months, CALC:risk_indicators), commercial inventories are depressed at 410M barrels (NOTE:B3), and the Strait of Hormuz conflict is actively escalating with naval mines striking tankers on Nov 26 (NOTE:E7) and Houthi drone strikes on Saudi refineries (NOTE:E16). EIA forecasts Brent to average near $100/bbl through year-end (NOTE:B1), suggesting modest upward drift from current Brent $91.80 (FRED:DCOILBRENTEU: 91.8) and WTI $82.24 (FRED:DCOILWTICO: 82.24).

dollar.why: The trade-weighted dollar index is strong at 123.6 (FRED:DTWEXBGS: 123.6). Although US yields are high (FRED:DGS2: 4.61), trade deficit remains very wide at -$105B (FRED:BOPGSTB: -105047). Current pricing reflects the interest rate differential; we maintain a neutral 0% forecast.

credit.why: High-yield credit spreads have experienced an acute blowout to 3.77% (z=+2.01 vs 5-year history, FRED:BAMLH0A0HYM2: 3.77), crossing into unusual territory and triggering the portfolio tripwire. With equity volatility elevated (VIX at 26.8, FRED:VIXCLS: 26.8) and S&P 500 in a downtrend below its 200-day moving average (-0.8%, CALC:risk_indicators), credit stress (measured as HYG/IEF) will face continued pressure/widening over the next 4 weeks.

evidence.value: High-yield credit spread=3.77 (96th percentile since 2023; widening fast)

inflation_exp.why: 10-year breakevens are well-anchored at 2.15% (FRED:T10YIE: 2.15) and wage growth has cooled to 3.12% (FRED:CES0500000003: 3.12). Despite high current CPI of 4.08% (FRED:CPIAUCSL: 4.08), market inflation expectations are already priced around long-run Fed targets (FACT:SEP_JCXFEMD_2029: 2).

scenarios.name: base
scenarios.description: Reflation persists with resilient domestic growth (GDP 4.3%) and sticky inflation (CPI 4.08%). The Fed stays on hold at the December 8-9 FOMC, while credit spread widening keeps financial risk appetite cautious.

scenarios.name: downside
scenarios.description: Credit spread blowout accelerates as high yields (30-yr mortgage at 7.21%, 10y at 4.85%) exacerbate private sector defaults, pulling the equity market into a formal correction with VIX spiking over 35.

scenarios.name: upside
scenarios.description: Oil supply pressures ease after the Nov 29 OPEC+ meeting, container freight rates continue falling (WCI down 3% to $4,032), inflation cools rapidly, and credit spreads compress back below 3.0%.

Financials.counterargument: Bank tightening standards have eased to 1.7% (FRED:DRTSCILM: 1.7), suggesting lending expansion could support an overweight.

critic.summary: No tilt is clearly unsupported or contradicted, so none fails. But most non-zero tilts rest on one factor call: further credit widening (only Sonnet -2 and Gemini -1.5; Opus and Grok at 0), multiplied by each sector's credit sensitivity. That is a concentrated, correlated bet, and counter-evidence (strong profits, easing bank standards, loose NFCI) is only weakly weighed. Staples and Utilities carry the two full +2 tilts despite negative same-regime history. Materials and Real Estate are flagged because their tilts are mechanical credit-beta artifacts that run against sector fundamentals and history.

Technology.issue: The -1 follows from Tech's highest credit sensitivity (SENS 1.38) and the widening-credit view. History is mildly positive but flat; momentum is already very negative. Capped, so the size is reasonable.

Financials.issue: Neutral is consistent with offsetting evidence: loan growth and a positive curve against flattening T10Y2Y and HY widening. Sonnet's own -0.044 credit sensitivity shows it is not credit-driven.

Health Care.issue: The +1 comes from the defensive credit sensitivity (-1.75) and strong momentum. Regime history is flat, which limits conviction, but the cap at +1 is appropriate.

Energy.issue: The +1 is supported by strong 3m regime history, steep backwardation and the Hormuz escalation. Counter-evidence is acknowledged (IEA supply surplus, oil -5% over 3m, 1m momentum -4.2). Much of the factor score comes from the credit coefficient rather than oil, since the net oil forecast is only about +1.75%, so conviction is modest.

Industrials.issue: Neutral with no real catalyst; positive history is offset by Section 301 ambiguity and weak shipping demand.

Consumer Discretionary.issue: The -1 rests on the credit/rates factors plus a -0.5 sentiment adjustment (UMCSENT 48, 1.64th percentile). Hard data (retail sales +6.82%, strong momentum) cuts the other way, and the counterargument is acknowledged. Sonnet misreads the sign of the inflation-expectation sensitivity: a falling forecast hurts this sector, it does not help. The sizing is small, so this does not change the tilt.

Consumer Staples.issue: The +2 is entirely credit-factor driven (SENS -2.46). Regime history is negative (3m -1.29%, 37.8% beat), and three of four models gave no sector-specific points. A full tilt on a two-model credit call is aggressive. Strong momentum and elevated VIX are consistent, but confidence is thinner than the +2 implies.

Utilities.issue: The +2 is again mostly the credit coefficient (-2.23) and the inflation-expectation decline. Regime history is negative (3m -1.23%, 39.6% beat) and there is no sector-specific support. Utilities and Staples are the same defensive credit-hedge bet, so the exposure is doubled up at full size.

Materials.issue: The +1 is an artifact of a negative credit coefficient (-0.77) on a cyclical commodity sector. All models gave 0 sector-specific points, same-regime history is negative at every window (3m -0.9%, 40% beat), and the copper and trade-policy data are stale. A cyclical sector gaining from credit stress is economically dubious, and Sonnet's own rationale found no supporting catalyst. Neutral would be more defensible.

Real Estate.issue: The +1 is credit-factor driven (SENS -1.03), but the sector-specific evidence points the other way. Mortgage rate is 7.21% (91.8th percentile), permits are at the 0th percentile, the 1m/3m regime history is negative, and the starting probability is 45% on a small n of 27. Sonnet's -3 housing-finance adjustment was dropped by the median. The tilt is not contradicted outright but is weakly grounded.

Communication Services.issue: Neutral is consistent with low factor sensitivities and mixed history and momentum.
